title: Sparse Configuration Interaction for the Electronic Schrödinger Equation Revisited: Complete Basis Set Limit Complexity and Quantum-Encoding Impact
abstract: In this article we revisit regularity results for eigenfunctions in the discrete spectrum of the electronic Schrödinger equation and study their consequences for approximation complexity. In particular, for the convergence to the complete basis set limit, it can be shown that the curse of dimensionality in the leading algebraic exponent can be mitigated. That is, for general sparse grid constructions, the main term of the convergence rate with respect to the number of degrees of freedom is independent of the number of electrons. These insights indicate potential benefits for classical numerical solvers of the electronic Schrödinger equation and also for quantum-computing approaches through new qubit-efficient wavefunction encodings.
summary: The paper develops Sparse Configuration Interaction (SCI) methods to solve the electronic Schrödinger equation by rigorously analyzing function spaces using Meyer wavelets. It proves that SCI mitigates the curse of dimensionality in basis set expansions, leading to convergence rates independent of electron number $N$. This breakthrough offers a path toward simulating strongly correlated systems with drastically reduced computational scaling for both classical and quantum computing platforms.
main_problem: To develop rigorous, scalable approximation methods for solving the electronic Schrödinger equation by mitigating the curse of dimensionality inherent in full configuration interaction (FCI) expansions.
main_result: The proposed Sparse Configuration Interaction (SCI) method achieves convergence rates to the complete basis set limit that are independent of the number of electrons ($N$), significantly reducing computational scaling compared to conventional methods.
method: The work combines advanced mathematical tools, including Meyer wavelet analysis on weighted Sobolev spaces defined over the $N$-particle domain, with quantum chemistry techniques like SCI and sparse grid approximations.
model_or_system: The system is governed by the electronic Schrödinger equation for interacting electrons in a molecular or atomic environment. The Hamiltonian involves electron-electron repulsion, electron-nucleus attraction, and nuclear repulsion terms.
key_observables: Convergence rate to the Complete Basis Set (CBS) limit; approximation error ($\|\Psi_{	ext{s}} - \Psi_{	ext{BFCI}}\|_{H^1}$); required number of qubits for quantum encoding ($n_{SCI}^q$).
important_parameters: Number of electrons ($N$); size of the one-particle basis set ($K$ or $L$); smoothness indices ($t, r$); and the degree of approximation (related to grid level $L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on establishing norm equivalences using Meyer wavelets in mixed-regularity weighted Sobolev spaces; it assumes that the underlying eigenfunctions possess sufficient regularity properties.
figures_summary: Notes reference comparisons showing SCI dramatically reduces determinant space dimensions and required qubits compared to FCI across various molecules (e.g., H2, FeMoco).
paper_structure: The paper builds mathematically by first characterizing function spaces using Meyer wavelets on the $N$-particle domain (Chunks 3 & 4), then applies these tools to derive error bounds for sparse grid approximations (Chunk 7), and finally translates these mathematical findings into computational scaling improvements for both classical solvers and quantum algorithms via SCI (Chunks 1, 2, 5, 6).
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework showing how advanced functional analysis techniques can overcome fundamental exponential scaling barriers in many-body physics simulations, directly impacting the feasibility of simulating complex chemical systems on both classical and quantum hardware.
